summary: IETF review teams check Internet-Drafts for things like general, security, operations, applications and routing issues as they move toward becoming RFCs. This informational RFC lists requirements for better integrating the tools that assign and track those reviews with the Datatracker, without disrupting how the teams already work.

plainLanguage.summary: Many helpers check a school project before it is finished. This lists what a better sign-up sheet would need so everyone knows who is checking what.

questions: how do ietf review teams work
what is soft hiatus for reviewers
subtitle: Integration requirements for IETF review team tools and the Datatracker.

tldr.problem: IETF review teams use a separate tool to assign and track reviews of Internet-Drafts, but it has its own data store and scrapes the Datatracker to learn about documents, creating redundancy and friction.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies requirements for reimplementing the review tool with tighter integration to the Datatracker so it can reuse credentials, automatically identify documents ready for review, and associate completed reviews without manual data entry.
tldr.outcome: A more integrated system would simplify workflows for team secretaries, reviewers, and document editors while maintaining the team structures and processes that have worked for years.

facts.label: Review teams mentioned
facts.value: Gen-ART, SecDir, AppsDir, OPS-dir, RTG-dir, MIB Doctors, YANG Doctors

today: RFC 7735 is an Informational specification published in January 2016. It documents requirements for the review tool infrastructure that IETF teams use to manage their review processes, though the specific tool implementation continues to evolve.

sections.title: Review Process and Current Tools
sections.content:
As Internet-Drafts progress toward becoming RFCs, several IETF review teams perform specialized reviews. The General Area Review Team (Gen-ART) does general technical reviews at Last Call. The Security Directorate (SecDir) reviews security implications. The Applications Area Directorate, Operations Area Directorate, Routing Area Directorate, and other specialized groups (MIB Doctors, YANG Doctors) review documents in their domains. Each team has a secretary who manages a pool of volunteer reviewers, assigns documents, tracks progress, and collects completed reviews.

RFC 7735 was written to capture requirements for improving the tool these teams use, developed by Tero Kivinen. The tool currently keeps its own data store and learns about documents by parsing Datatracker and tools.ietf.org pages. Tighter integration would simplify this data collection, allow reuse of Datatracker credentials, and make it easier to detect review-triggering events like a Working Group Last Call.
sections.plainLanguage: Several teams of reviewers check drafts at different stages. They use a tool to organize the work, but the tool reads information the hard way by scraping web pages. A better tool would get information directly from the main Datatracker.

sections.title: Secretary and Reviewer Workflows
sections.content:
Team secretaries typically work once a week, checking the tool for documents ready for review based on Last Call announcements and IESG Telechat agendas. The secretary creates a set of assignments in one atomic unit, assigning reviewers in roughly round-robin order but accounting for reviewer availability, vacations, and avoiding conflicts (not assigning an author, shepherd, or WG chair to review their own work). This assignment process can take several minutes, and new Last Calls may arrive while the secretary is working.

Some teams like the Routing Area Directorate use a review-on-demand model, where reviews are initiated at the request of an AD or WG chair. Reviewers discover assignments through email or the tool, and can reject assignments by coordinating with the secretary through email. After completing a review, the reviewer sends it to the team's email list and other relevant lists, then indicates completion and the review location in the tool. The SecDir secretary often manually collects review links from email because waiting for documents to appear in the archive to find the link is cumbersome.
sections.plainLanguage: Every week the secretary picks who should check each draft, trying to be fair and avoiding conflicts. Reviewers get told by email, do the review, send it to the email list, and tell the tool it is done.

sections.title: Secretary-Focused Requirements
sections.content:
Secretaries need to see what documents are ready for review of a given type (Last Call, Telechat, early review). They must be able to work on and issue a set of assignments as one atomic unit, with warnings if multiple secretaries try to work simultaneously. The tool should make it easy to discover new documents ready for review while an assignment set is being created. It should help generate assignment emails to the team's email list, allow marking documents as "no review expected," and show next available reviewers in order.

Secretaries need to view and edit reviewer availability (frequency, not-available-until dates, skip-next-n-assignments), see which team members have requested to review a document, and identify that a reviewer is already involved with a draft (through roles or regular expressions matching draft names). They need to see key features of documents (length, authors, title, abstract, IESG and WG states, shepherd, already-assigned reviewers). The tool must easily show the results of previous reviews of the same document or replaced documents, recent reviewer performance statistics, and allow follow-up reminders when actions are due.
sections.plainLanguage: The secretary's tool needs to show what is ready, let her assign reviewers fairly, show her who has done what before, and remind her when something is overdue.

sections.title: Reviewer-Focused Requirements
sections.content:
Reviewers must be able to indicate availability as maximum reviews per week/fortnight/month/quarter, and declare hiatus periods. A soft hiatus means no new assignments but finish existing ones. A hard hiatus means reassign everything. Reviewers should also indicate transition to inactive status with a deadline, after which the secretary reassigns outstanding work.

Reviewers need to easily discover new assignments (via direct email or in-tool notification), see current outstanding, completed, and rejected assignments clearly, and optionally request to review a particular document at any stage. They must be able to reject assignments (with explanation), indicate they have accepted and are working on one, request additional reviewers if a review will be only partial, and mark a review complete with its location in archives and result summary. The tool should track which document version was reviewed, especially when a document is revised between assignment and completion. Reviewers should receive email reminders when reviews are about to become overdue.
sections.plainLanguage: Reviewers need to say when they are busy, get told about their assignments, be able to say yes or no or ask for help, finish the review, and remember which version they reviewed.

sections.title: Datatracker Integration and Statistics
sections.content:
Review requesters (ADs and WG chairs) must be able to request any type of review easily and withdraw requests. When viewing a document's main page in the Datatracker, it must be easy to find all reviews of that document with links to review text and related discussion. For documents that replace other documents, reviews of the replaced documents should appear in the results.

The tool must provide statistics across all teams, a given team, or a given reviewer, for all time or over configurable periods: count of completed reviews, in-progress reviews, late reviews, uncompleted reviews, and average completion time. Statistics should show review counts by result type (ready, ready with nits, not ready, etc.) and account for document length. Access should be configurable: Secretariat and ADs see any statistic; team secretaries see their team's; reviewers see team aggregates and their own statistics.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone should be able to see all reviews of any draft. The system should show how many reviews each team completes, how late they usually are, and let them spot reviewers who are overwhelmed.
